1.pericope_label: The command to rear up the tabernacle

schools.summary: Gill sets the scene from the close of the last chapter: the tabernacle and all its work were finished, and Moses had taken a survey of everything belonging to it, which appeared to be done as had been ordered.

Henry reads the whole command as an order of assembly and consecration and draws a lesson from each stage — that Moses would not erect the tabernacle until he had express orders, so that it is good to see God going before us in every step; that the placing came before the anointing, since every thing was sanctified when it was put in its proper place and not till then, for as every thing is beautiful in its season so is every thing in its place; that the consecration of the men followed the consecration of the things, as goods brought into a house are marked first and clean servants then hired to bear the vessels of the Lord; and that in half a year the tabernacle was completed, since when the hearts of numbers are earnest in a good cause much may be done in a short time.
Clarke fixes the moment on the calendar, dating the command to set up the tabernacle to the first day of the first month of the second year of their departure from Egypt.

2.pericope_label: The first day of the first month

schools.summary: Gill names the month as Nisan, on the Targum of Jonathan's authority, and dates the interval — the same month in which Israel came out of Egypt, out of which they had now been a whole year excepting fourteen days. Calvin refuses the premise the whole computation rests on: he cannot at all approve the opinion that the tabernacle was only now set up, since it was complete in all its parts before Moses went the second time into the mount and had stood pitched outside the camp in token of divorce ever since the calf; what the setting-up means is that it was fixed in its right and legitimate place, in the midst of the people to whom it had been a stranger.

Clarke takes it as generally supposed that the work began about the sixth month after leaving Egypt and finished near the close of the first year, so that six months went into the making and the tabernacle stood erected one year all but fifteen days after the exodus — a building of such curious and costly workmanship as was never got up in so short a time, but the work of the Lord, and the people had a mind to work. Wesley adds the precedent of Hezekiah, who began sanctifying the temple on the first day of the first month, and notes that the new moon opening every month was kept with solemnity, so that this first new moon of the year was the more remarkable.

Ellicott counts the stages — the fourteenth of Abib for the exodus, the third month for the arrival at Sinai, nearly three months for the two long absences of Moses in the mount — and concludes that the sixth or seventh month had come before the work commenced and the eleventh or twelfth before it was finished, which is why the approaching new year offered its first day for the inauguration; he also corrects the title to the tabernacle, the tent of meeting, the two words standing in apposition rather than in regimen.

debates: Whether the tabernacle was first set up on this day at all. Calvin holds that it was already complete before Moses' second ascent and had been pitched outside the camp in token of divorce since the golden calf, so that the setting-up means its restoration to its proper place in the midst of the people — against the commentators who read the verse as the erection of a new structure, which is how Clarke and Ellicott reckon the dates.
themes: beginning the year with a good work

3.pericope_label: The furniture placed and the whole anointed

schools.summary: Gill identifies each object and the room it belonged to — the ark where the law was, set in the most holy place; the shewbread table in the holy place; the golden altar not inside the most holy place but over against it; the altar of burnt offering in the open court, as was proper both because of the smell and the smoke of the sacrifices; the court's hangings on all four sides — and gives the scope of the anointing that follows. Calvin will not let the oil be mistaken for the thing it stands for: there was no efficacy for sanctification in it except as a type of the Spirit, from whom as its only source all holiness emanates, so that the figure teaches that nothing pleases God except what the Spirit has purged and consecrated; and he answers the question why the altar alone is called most holy, from the sacrifices, which are so called on account of the expiation made by them.
Clarke reads the command to set in order the things upon the table as placing the twelve loaves there in the order described earlier in the book.

Ellicott notes that the most precious object goes in first and is immediately covered with the veil; agrees that the twelve loaves are the things intended while doubting whether the frankincense is glanced at; qualifies the lighting of the lamps as at the close of the day; places the golden altar outside the veil but nearer to it than table or candlestick; explains the laver's position by the priests' washing at every entrance; and points back to the earlier legislation both for the composition of the oil and for the list of things to be consecrated by it.

themes: the Spirit as the source of holiness

schools.summary: Gill states the purpose of bringing them to the door — to be washed, anointed and clothed, that they might minister in the priest's office — and observes that the sequence was fixed, Aaron anointed first and his sons after him. Calvin marks a distinction of stages, that Aaron had been appointed priest before and is now at length inaugurated so as to begin the discharge of his office, and insists that the oil was consecrated by God; from which he turns on the Popish bishops who ape Moses by sprinkling their priests and altars with stinking oil, since this ceremony belonged to the ancient shadows and ceased at the coming of Christ. He adds Augustine's observation that Moses, commissioned to anoint the others, was never consecrated by any visible symbol himself — proof that outward signs are not estimated by the dignity of the minister but only by the ordinance of God.

Clarke traces the everlasting priesthood forward until it runs out: the anointing gave Aaron's family a right to the high priesthood for ever without repetition of the unction, yet the high priest himself was anointed at his consecration, and that continued to the destruction of the first temple and, on the authority of Eusebius and Cyril of Jerusalem, among the Jews until the advent of our Lord — after which there is no evidence of it, the true priest and the true sacrifice being come. Wesley says more briefly that the unction sealed their priesthood for as long as the Jewish polity lasted and sufficed for all succeeding priests, none being anointed afterwards but the high priests.

Ellicott notes that ablution, investiture and anointing had all been appointed already, would render the sons' garments tunics rather than coats, and establishes from Leviticus that the manner differed between father and sons — Aaron had the oil poured over his head, his sons were merely sprinkled with a mixture of oil and blood, a difference implying a lower degree of official holiness; he also reports the Jewish commentators' rule that the single anointing of the sons sufficed for all time while each high priest was inducted by anointing, whence the title the anointed priest.

16.pericope_label: Thus did Moses: the tabernacle reared

schools.summary: Gill sums the execution in a line and dates it to the first month of the second year of the departure out of Egypt. Calvin presses the repeated formula into a polemic: it must be especially noted that Moses obeyed so as not to vary in the most trifling point from the form prescribed him, and that he so frequently enforces the fact — not without reason, for there is nothing to which men are more prone than mixing their own inventions with God's commands, as if they would be wiser than he. If so great a prophet dared attempt nothing of himself in trifling matters, how great is the audacity of those who arbitrarily invent innumerable figments whereby God may be worshipped.

Henry argues from where the work was done: they did not put off rearing the tabernacle till they came to Canaan, though they hoped to be there shortly, but set it up in the midst of their camp in the wilderness — so that those unsettled in the world must not think this excuses their continued irreligion, a tabernacle for God being a needful companion even in a wilderness, especially considering that our carcases may fall in that wilderness. He also observes that Moses did all God directed and in the order God appointed, the words as the Lord commanded Moses recurring seven times in less than fourteen verses, and that great as he was Moses would not vary from the institution in the least punctilio.

Ellicott separates what the verse asserts from what it does not: it states generally that Moses carried out the whole series of instructions but says nothing about when, the following passage fixing only the first set to the first day of the second year while Leviticus shows the rest were executed later. He also explains the speed of the erection from the builders rather than the building — the tabernacle was made to be rapidly put together and taken to pieces, and the family of Abraham had been familiar with tent life from Ur onwards and kept that familiarity in Egypt on the borders of the desert.

debates: When the instructions were carried out. Ellicott holds that this verse's general statement covers the whole series but that only the erection (vv. 2-8) belongs to the first day of the second year, the anointing and the consecration of the priests being deferred to the events of Leviticus 8; Henry keeps the same distinction in plainer terms, making the rearing one day's work and the consecrating a matter of some days after.

18.pericope_label: The frame, the coverings and the testimony

schools.summary: Gill enters a qualification on the verb — Moses reared up the tabernacle not of himself but with the help of others — and takes the tent spread abroad over it to be the curtains of goats' hair.

Clarke reads the same word more broadly, understanding by the tent, here and elsewhere, the coverings made of rams' skins, goats' hair and the rest which were thrown over the building, for the tabernacle had no other kind of roof.

Ellicott rests the whole stability of the structure on the sockets, which were of considerable weight but cannot by mere weight have held the fabric upright, so that they were probably let into the ground to a depth of some feet; once fixed, the boards and pillars were inserted by their tenons and the bars riveted the three walls into one compact structure. He also separates the two terms of the verse, the goats'-hair covering being the true tent that roofed the dwelling and the covering above it the outer protection of rams' and seals' skins. Keil and Delitzsch fix the sense of the testimony placed in the ark as the decalogue written on the two tables of stone, the phrase standing as an abbreviation for the tables of testimony, and note that the veil was hung only after the ark had been brought in.

debates: What the tent spread over the tabernacle was. Gill takes it for the goats'-hair curtains, Clarke for all the coverings of skins and hair thrown over the building, and Ellicott distinguishes the two clauses — the goats' hair being the tent proper and the rams' and seals' skins the outer covering laid above it.
outliers: Knobel understood the testimony put into the ark as the revelation so far as it then existed, that is, the instructions for the sanctuary and the priesthood; Keil and Delitzsch reject the reading as arbitrary and hold to the decalogue on the two tables.

20.pericope_label: The ark, the table, the candlestick and the golden altar

schools.summary: Gill explains the name of the testimony — the ten commands, so called because they testified and declared what the will of God was with respect to things to be done and not done — doubts the Targum of Jonathan's claim that the broken pieces of the first tables were put in with them, has the twelve cakes set in two rows, six in a row, distinguishes the golden altar from the brazen by its overlay, and notes that Moses lighted the lamps himself because Aaron and his sons were not yet invested with their office, so that in this and several other things in the chapter he officiated as a priest.
Clarke identifies the testimony as the two tables on which the ten commandments had been written.

Ellicott specifies the tables of stone written with the finger of God which Moses brought down from Sinai on his last visit, declines to conclude from the verse that the ark held nothing but the testimony, fixes the sides by the position of a man facing the veil and gives the reason for the arrangement — the light would thus be thrown on the table of shewbread — and suggests Moses may have known the right placing from the pattern shewed him in the mount. Keil and Delitzsch describe the room as a plan with a centre and two sides, and object to the usual rendering of the Hebrew for the shewbread, which signifies not a row of bread but the position or placing of bread.

debates: Whether the ark held anything besides the tables. Gill reports and rejects the Targum of Jonathan's claim that the broken pieces of the first tables were laid in it, holding that no tables were put in except those Moses hewed by God's order; Ellicott declines to settle it from this verse, which he says does not prove that the ark held nothing but the testimony.
themes: the arrangement of the holy place

27.pericope_label: The incense, the brazen altar, the laver and the court

schools.summary: Gill reads the burning of the incense as another branch of the priestly office exercised by Moses, one he would never have undertaken without a command from God for it; notes that the hanging went up at the door of the holy place once everything to be placed there had been brought in; explains that Moses, officiating as a priest, washed at the laver along with Aaron and his sons, whom he was about to consecrate and invest by offering sacrifice for them, citing Jarchi for the eighth day of the consecration; and gives the court its dimensions from the earlier chapter.

Ellicott ties the incense and the lamps to a single hour, at even, argues that a preposition has fallen out before the word door — the translators supplying the one meaning at, where he thinks the word used earlier in the chapter and rendered before is the likelier omission, so that the altar stood not at the door but in front of it — and identifies what was offered on it as the first evening sacrifice, a lamb with its prescribed meat offering. Keil and Delitzsch note that water was put in the laver to wash with, and that Moses and Aaron and his sons alike washed both on entering the tent of meeting and on approaching the altar.

debates: What preposition has dropped out before the word door. The translators supplied the particle meaning at; Ellicott argues from the parallel earlier in the chapter that the omitted word is the one rendered before, so that the altar of burnt offering stood in front of the door rather than at it.

34.pericope_label: The cloud covered the tent and the glory filled it

schools.summary: Gill identifies the cloud with the pillar that had gone before Israel almost from their coming out of Egypt, now appearing not erect but expanded so as to cover the tabernacle outside. Calvin takes the sign as proof rather than ornament: the people knew by this pledge that the tabernacle had not been set up in vain but that the earlier promise was fulfilled, for it was not natural that a cloud should settle over the sanctuary, much less that cloud and fire should alternate perpetually; and he notices the reversal in Moses' own case, the cloud that had once concealed him from the people now keeping even him outside, by whose example Levites and multitude alike were warned not to press further than allowed.

Henry begins at creation — as God, having finished the earth, made man and put him in possession of it, so when Moses had finished the tabernacle God came and took possession — and reads the tokens as the return of a favour forfeited by the golden calf, concluding that God will dwell with those that prepare him a habitation. He puts the cloud to four uses: a token of presence visible to the remotest corners of the camp, a concealment, a protection better than all the coverings beneath it, and a guide. Of the fire within he presses both mercy and terror — the curtains no more singed than the bush was consumed, yet the light so dazzling that Moses waited at the door until the splendour abated, which Moses could not do but our Lord Jesus has done as forerunner.

Clarke reads the event as a verdict on the work, God giving his approbation of it in a token visible to all the people, and marks a removal — the cloud had rested on the provisional tent Moses pitched outside the camp after the molten calf, and now left it for this tabernacle, which he believes stood at the centre of the camp with the twelve tribes pitching around it. Wesley follows Henry almost sentence for sentence.

Ellicott notes that the Hebrew has the cloud, the same that directed their journeys from Succoth, and separates the verse's two halves — the cloud resting on the tent outside while the glory, some ineffably brilliant appearance, entered within and filled the dwelling, God thereby declaring his intention of keeping the promise to go with the people in person.

35.pericope_label: The cloud by day and the fire by night

schools.summary: Gill explains that Moses had already been within, in the holy place and the most holy, and had come out, and could not now engage his heart or find boldness to go in until he should be called; describes the cloud rising into the form of a pillar and going before them; draws from the rule that they did not journey while it rested the observation that it might rest two days, a month or a year, which goes some way to account for the long continuance of Israel in the wilderness; and takes the daytime cloud and the nighttime fire for one phenomenon differently lit, serving as shelter from the sun, direction of the way, and perhaps a terror to wild beasts. Calvin agrees on the necessity of the change, since the cloud would not have been visible amidst the darkness, and gets his best point from the second explanation the verse adds — that had the cloud daily accomplished the same course the very regularity would have obscured the power of God, whereas by resting a whole year and then pointing out now a longer journey and now a shorter it manifested the paternal care of God the more conspicuously.

Clarke refers the subject of the last three verses back to his treatment of the pillar of cloud and fire at the exodus, and carries the token as far as it went: a merciful providence and a proof of the divinity of their religion, never withdrawn despite their repeated disobedience until they came into the promised land, after which, the tabernacle being fixed, it was confined to the holy of holies upon the mercy-seat until the first temple was destroyed and was no more seen in Israel till God was manifested in the flesh — the influences it figures being necessary not for a time only but through all our journeys.

Ellicott reconstructs the moment at the door: seeing the cloud descend as it had upon the temporary tent of meeting, Moses apparently tried to re-enter the tabernacle he had just quitted and could not, the glory forbidding approach as it did the priests when it descended on Solomon's temple.

themes: the pillar of cloud and fire
